title: Beyond Shelter: Lydia's House and the Power of Hospitality
author: Alysse ElHage
summary: Alysse ElHage interviews Mary Ellen Mitchell, co-founder of Lydia's House, a Catholic Worker house of hospitality in Norwood, Ohio, that serves pregnant and parenting women under 30. Mitchell describes how a shelter grew into twelve affordable apartments, a day care and ongoing family programming. She argues that poverty is the central problem but that housing and jobs alone are not enough, because a single mother who does everything by herself remains vulnerable. She proposes more imaginative shared living, such as two mothers sharing a home or a young mother living with a relative, and questions whether independence should always be the highest goal. The interview closes on father-hunger: Mitchell has seen boys light up around male volunteers and argues that boys need to see men keep commitments and show up consistently. It is a practitioner's account and anecdotal rather than a study.
points: Lydia's House grew from a single shelter into 12 income-based apartments, a day care and aftercare, forming a community of families who stay connected.
Employment and housing problems reinforce each other for single mothers, so job placement alone is not enough if she is still the only responsible adult.
Mitchell argues that the expectation that one income and one adult can cover rent, child care and all parenting is itself part of the housing crisis.
She questions whether independent housing should always be the goal and suggests shared households as one answer.
Children at the house respond strongly to male volunteers, which she takes as evidence that boys especially need dependable men who show up consistently.
quotes: What began as one house has become a community of families who stay connected over time.
We hear anger from the moms but also a great deal of sadness, as the fathers let them and their kids move into a shelter.

So, it’s not enough to help a single mother find a job. We have to ask: how she can keep that job while being the person responsible for everything in her child’s life? When employment becomes unstable, housing does too; the two problems reinforce each other.
We've created a supportive enclave of mothers and children, yet it is also a place where men are largely absent. That's become an important question for me.
One of the biggest problems with single parenting is the single part. There is a math problem that comes with a single income supporting a family.
Another dependable adult can make it possible to keep a job when a child is sick, share rent, or simply get through an exhausting day.
I’ve become convinced that human behavior is catching: we learn how to be human by watching other humans. Boys need to see men being fathers, employees, neighbors, and dependable people.
More than volunteers who show up weekly, or a living commune that might include men, our kids need dads.
